evidence.title: Reciprocal adjustment is observed in a short human–robot task
evidence.observation: Source-reported finding: A bounded-memory model adjusts robot policy to estimated human willingness to adapt. In a simulated table-carrying study with 69 included participants, people were more likely to switch toward the robot strategy than under cross-training. Observation period and measurement context: Short simulated interactions; calendar dates not established.
evidence.evidence_standing: Source-reported bounded account; study or measurement; not independently reproduced
evidence.glossary_fit: Illustrative or qualifying; does not validate a definition
evidence.limitations: Mechanical Turk sample; participants initially preferring the robot goal excluded; discrete actions, specified rewards and short interaction. No significant satisfaction difference. Does not establish longitudinal organizational coevolution.
evidence.open_questions: Transfer to other populations, tasks and operating environments remains unestablished. Missing measurement details are not inferred.
evidence.support_assessment: Commons interpretation: A bounded experimental illustration of reciprocal adjustment, with task and model assumptions retained.
evidence.dispute_status: See source version and dispute qualifications; no systematic clearance claimed.
evidence.verification_status: Not independently verified by the Commons

terms.name: Human–AI mutual adaptation
terms.definition: Reciprocal changes in human practices and AI-enabled activities as each responds to the other. Delegation can change how people decide and work; human behavior and institutions can reshape AI adoption, incentives, and subsequent capabilities.

relationships.explanation: Illustrates reciprocal adjustment in a short controlled human–robot task, not long-term generative-AI coevolution.
